items.title: [AINews] Meta Connect 2026: Muse glasses, voice, video, and Charm
items.text:
Team Zuck is absolutely on fire. Here's a good supercut of Meta Connect:
 

 and the effusive praise on Stratechery shows the mood on the ground. Unfortunately, no MSL updates beyond a tease , since Muse Spark was launched 3 weeks ago . However, Muse itself counts as a success, since it has overtaken ChatGPT in the App Store , and more developments (email!) and integrations take away the sting of being blocked by Amazon .
 
 Lastly, it was nice to see Limitless, the last "stealth" MSL acquisition , re-emerge as Charm:
 
 
 AI News for 9/22/2026-9/23/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies!
 
 AI Twitter Recap Top Story: Meta Connect 2026: Muse personal agent, glasses hardware, and Muse Realtime Avatar 
 What happened Meta used Connect to present Muse, its personal agent, as the center of a hardware-plus-agent strategy. It shipped agent features and new glasses, and teased, but did not release, a new frontier model. 
 Keynote framing. @finkd set the keynote for 4pm PT and later posted a recap thread . Live-blogger @kimmonismus summarized the thesis as "personal Superintelligence coming soon," which means people need hardware to interact with it, so Meta is going all-in on AI glasses.

 Muse voice and real-time video. Muse now supports voice and real-time video. It can hold long conversations while working on tasks in the background ( @finkd ). Video chat with a prompt-customizable voice is marked "coming soon" ( @alexandr_wang ). The official account's teaser: "you gave your Muse a look. now give it a voice" ( @Muse ).

 Muse on glasses. Muse is coming to all Meta glasses, activated by saying its name (a wake word), "coming soon" ( @alexandr_wang ).

 Muse Mail. Each Muse gets its own email address. You can CC it on a thread or forward it items to handle ( @alexandr_wang ).

 Computer use on Mac. Muse for Mac now does computer use: "queue up your jobs, walk away, and it keeps going" ( @alexandr_wang ).

 Connectors and commerce. @alexandr_wang showed the connector catalog. Partner graphics were posted for Spotify , Box and an apparent Temu integration.

 Business model and partner list. @clairejyz compiled the numbers from the keynote:
 Muse is free for users, but Meta may eventually take a cut of transactions.

 Retail and commerce integrations: Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Instacart, and others.

 Productivity integrations: Box, GitHub, Granola, Notion.

 The connector platform has 1,500+ applications, including Lovable and ElevenLabs.

 
 Muse Realtime Avatar (research release). A new model animates your Muse in sync with Muse Realtime Voice. It answers in under a second and supports unbounded session length ( @alexandr_wang ; @AIatMeta ). All output is watermarked as AI "without adding latency" ( @alexandr_wang ). Meta calls it "the foundation for realtime, embodied AI across our products."

 Hardware. 
 Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3: longer battery, upgraded microphones, new styles including Aviators ( @finkd ).

 Meta VR Glasses: Meta's first VR delivered in glasses rather than a headset, pitched as private cinema, multi-monitor workstation and game console ( @finkd ). Price is $1,299 ( @kimmonismus ).

 Hearing aid: glasses have been turned into an FDA-cleared hearing aid ( @iScienceLuvr ).

 Muse Charm: a keychain device for talking to Muse, shipping in December ( @finkd ; @alexandr_wang ).

 
 Acquisition. WaveForms AI, the speech/audio startup led by Alexis Conneau, was acquired by Meta, and its work surfaced at Connect ( @alex_conneau ). This lines up with the real-time voice and avatar stack.

 Frontier model teased, not shipped. Wang said "pretty soon we are dropping the most capable model we have ever trained" ( @scaling01 ). Pre-event expectations of "big chungus muse models" ( @scaling01 ) were not met.

 Facts vs. opinions Verifiable or official claims: 
 Feature and device announcements from @finkd, @alexandr_wang, @AIatMeta and @Muse.

 The $1,299 VR Glasses price.

 December ship date for Muse Charm.

 FDA-cleared hearing-aid functionality.

 The partner and connector counts compiled by @clairejyz.

 Vendor-run evaluation, to treat with caution: 
 Meta compared Muse Realtime Avatar against Runway Characters and HeyGen LiveAvatar using each product's own live-call experience.

 Raters held 2–3 minute conversations with matched avatar identities. They judged visual quality, audio-visual sync, character consistency and mannerisms ( @AIatMeta ).

 Meta reports Muse "came out ahead on overall preference" but posted no margins or rater counts in the tweets. Wang himself added "［unsurprisingly］" ( @alexandr_wang ).

 Details are in the research blog .

 Promotional volume, not substance: 
 Wang posted a large stream of memes and shitposts through the night. Examples: "muse-inhood" and the "1 billion users" mem

items.title: Xi Descends on DC
items.text:
I joined ChinaTalk's for a wide-ranging conversation ahead of the Trump-Xi summit . We discuss: 
 Trump-Xi summit scenarios, Beijing's management of uncertainty and protocol , and how the script of US-China diplomacy has flipped, with things once seen as American concessions to China now treated as concessions from Beijing; 

 The K-shaped US-China relationship , with leader-level diplomacy pulling upward while competition pulls downward; 

 What Xi's visit says about the changing political salience of China in the US; 

 Why Beijing's public statements on AI risk don't necessarily tell us how it will handle pacing and safety; 

 What the decline of Xi Jinping could mean for a political system and why China's next succession could be especially difficult to predict; 

 Chinamaxxing from Kissinger to Trump; 

 Plus: The Scholars (儒林外史) and why Qing-dynasty satire about corrupt scholars might make you feel better about America in 2026. 

 Check it out here:
 ChinaTalk 
 Xi Descends on DC

 ChinaTalk book club is happening in SF! The first book we're reading is Xiao Hai's Adrift in the South, and we've partnered with a local bookstore to supply copies — in SF or online. You can RSVP and find out more on Luma. We hope to see you there…

items.title: A piece in the New Yorker on the “But China” problem; why China will lose control of AI
items.text:
When I was a graduate student in philosophy, we constantly dealt in "thought experiments"—things like the Trolley Problem. These mental exercises strip away messy, real-world complications to explore new moral terrain. One famous example is Peter Singer's image of the drowning child , which helped argue forcefully why distance and visibility are not relevant factors for moral responsibility.
 The trouble with thought experiments is that they can erase so much of the real world that little of practical use survives. In the Trolley Problem, when in real-life have you ever been certain an action you make will kill one person to save five? If there was any uncertainty, would you pull the lever? Herein lies the crux of the issue: If we wouldn't leave philosophers alone at the head of a moving train, should we leave the philosopher-engineers in charge of whether America should pause or accelerate AI development?
 In a piece for the New Yorker today , I write about the problems with evoking China as the reason to avoid pausing or slowing down AI development and regulation. The argument, sometimes called "But China" is rooted in a thought experiment: it takes a sensible premise like self-improving AI and slips into absurdity—killer robots, ethnically targeted bioweapons—while ignoring basic realities of how complicated it is for technologies to diffuse through societies and organizations. As has argued powerfully, the AI "race" is a marathon, not a sprint. Even god, if it is to mean something in this world, must come down to earth and grapple with all its messiness.
 The EA inheritance Singer's drowning-child arguments helped launch the effective altruism movement, the dominant ideational force behind America's current AI drive. Among its most influential figures is the Oxford philosopher Nick Bostrom, who, in 2018, published a book on superintelligence. In one thought experiment in that book, Bostrom imagines a nation's AI project beginning to recursively self-improve, pulling far enough ahead of its competitors to "achieve complete world domination." He called this a "decisive strategic advantage."
 In the years since Trump 2.0 made an alliance with the tech elite, the concept of decisive strategic advantage has fused with the DC national security establishment to become America's ultimate boogeyman: the unifying menace of a China "winning" the AI race. This is now the only thing standing in the way of urgent calls to slowdown AI development and it has apparently become so scary that people prefer "we're all gonna die" to whatever is coming out of China. As Ted Cruz put the point succinctly: "If there are gonna be killer robots, I'd rather they be American killer robots than Chinese killer robots." 
 Aside from all the reasons I cited in the piece about technological diffusion, I don't believe the line between Chinese AI companies, who are clearly committed to global partnerships, and the PLA are that porous. In my experience Chinese businessmen are almost always excited to have their products shipped and recognized by the West and they have only mentioned the prospect of working with the Communist Party when they expect to be sanctioned or cannot succeed in that endeavor. What's more, none of the evidence in the Chinese AI landscape suggests to me that China's leaders care or even see superintelligence like the West—for example, I don't see the AI 2027 prediction of China creating a Manhattan project for AI coming to pass. (It was predicted to happen this year. I don't think we're even close.)
 While I'm convinced that the risks of China pulling ahead in AI development have been grossly exaggerated compared to dealing first with America's urgent problems of AI-misalignment, I'm inclined to believe researchers like Jacob Coxon who say AI can cause catastrophic harm given all the existing evidence since the Hugging Face incident. The risk of China using such powerful AI systems to dominate the world are overblown, but whether China will lose control of AI is a different matter and I'm dedicating the rest of this post to share my views about why I think they will. (I apologize for the length.) 
 The perils of Chinese silence For the past few years, I've struggled to write about Chinese AI safety issues. On the one hand, one has to give credit where credit is due. When I started covering Chinese tech in 2020, coverage was pretty ethically straight-forward: Beijing was disappearing businessmen and vaporizing entire industries like private tutoring. I don't think I met a single Chinese beyond chest-thumping nationalists who thought the early tech crackdowns were a good idea. Given that starting point, it's impressive how far tech regulations have come since then as has covered so extensively. Some Chinese leaders clearly recognized that they cannot keep playing whack-a-mole with the most dynamic sector in their economy and did something about. The results of this are already quite impressive.

items.title: Putin’s campaign against Europe
items.text:
Russia is stepping up its campaign to weaken Europe and undermine its support for Ukraine. We asked Dr. Hanna Notte to provide an assessment of what is going on and how European countries should respond. Dr. Notte is Eurasia program director at the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies and has fellowships at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and the Kennan Institute in Washington, DC. 
 Her latest book "We Shall Outlast Them: Putin's Global Campaign to Defeat the West" provides an informed, gripping but also alarming account of how Russian foreign policy has sought to weaken the West in response to the support given to Ukraine. An opportunity to purchase a discounted copy of her book can be found at the end of this post. 
 
 


 
 Since February 2022, Russia's foreign statecraft has undergone an extraordinary transformation. Instead of reaping the fruits of a swift "special military operation", the Kremlin was forced just months into its invasion of Ukraine to prepare for a long, hard slog. Confronted with Western sanctions, Russian technocrats hustled to secure alternative trade conduits and lifelines for the country's economy and defense enterprise. Framing the war as "anti-neocolonial", propagandists wooed audiences in the Global South. And in multilateral institutions—old ones like the UN and newer ones such as BRICS—Russian diplomats sought to rally non-Western counterparts in support of their country's agenda. 
 Soon enough, Russia's engagement with the world became subservient to one single goal: Outlasting the West in Ukraine. Novelties and curiosities in Russian foreign policy resulted from this elevation of war as the chief organizing principle: There was innovation—with Russia's turn to Iran for Shahed drones, whose production it then localized in the Alabuga Special Economic Zone, enlisting unwitting African students (and, later, North Korean workers) in support. There was improvisation—with Russia's curation of a fleet of shadow tankers, which ended up not just transporting Russian oil but also serving as launchpads for a drone campaign across Europe. There was radicalization—with Russian pundits threatening Europe with nuclear war with almost soporific predictability. And sometimes, there was restraint—with President Putin abandoning his long-time ally Bashar al-Assad of Syria to his fall in December 2024. 
 Over 4.5 years into the war, Russia's versatile global efforts have produced an ambivalent balance sheet. On one hand, its non-Western partners have created a relatively permissive international environment for a war-waging Russia. Russia has sold record amounts of oil to India, diverted trade through the "Eurasian roundabout", imported North Korean missiles and munitions, and procured vast amounts of Chinese dual-use and other goods. Yet, the sum total of such international support, provided to Russia by die-hard and opportunistic abettors alike, has been insufficient to enable it to win the war. 
 What's more, even though Russia has eluded international isolation, its global power projection has eroded. Its Syrian bases, important pillars of its longstanding presence in the Middle East, are currently being downgraded. In the South Caucasus, Russia's traditional ally Armenia is looking for alternative partners. Just recently, Kazakhstan's President Tokayev and India's Prime Minister Modi publicly chided Putin over his forever war.
